Lab 008 · Lessons 008–009 · simulation using the lessons' numbers

Jobs Lab

Lesson 008: split the storm's 2,000,000 rain particles across up to 8 threads and watch each thread's row: blue is real work, red is fighting over a cache line, orange is queuing for a lock. Lesson 009: turn the whole frame into jobs and watch 8 cores fill up, or sit idle, depending on who waits for whom.

Storm finale, night city. Goal: the particle update under its 2.5 ms budget, so the GPU (14.5 ms) stays the slower side.

        What this shows
        
    
        
      
        The serial part sets the limit
        0.8 ms of FillHoles runs on one thread. With 8 threads the best is 0.8 + 8.0 ÷ 8 = 1.8 ms, a 4.9× speedup, not 8×.
        
      
        A lock makes threads take turns
        16,667 trips through one lock can't overlap. That 1.0 ms stays the same with 2 or 8 threads. Per-thread lists remove it.
        
      
        False sharing looks like work
        8 counters in one 64-byte line make every ++ pull the line from another core. No wait marker shows it; only the cost per particle does (10.4 ns vs 4.0 ns).
        
    
        
    
        
      
        A job is not parallel by itself
        Schedule() then Complete() at once makes the main thread wait for every job in turn. The work moved to Worker 1, but the frame got 0.3 ms slower: 13.41 ms.
        
      
        The longest chain sets the limit
        With the task graph, each job waits only for what it needs. The frame then can't beat its critical path: Gameplay → AI → Animation → Render prep = 8.8 ms. Batches shorten that chain: 5.64 ms.
        
      
        Job size has a sweet spot
        1 particle job leaves 7 cores idle (11.66 ms). 16,384 jobs keep the cores 68% busy, mostly with overhead (9.80 ms). Anything from 4 to 1,024 jobs is within 0.32 ms of the best.
        
    
        
    
        This lab is a simulation using Lesson 008's numbers, not a measurement: 4 ns of work per particle, 0.8 ms serial, 16,667 deaths per frame at about 60 ns per contended lock and 40 ns per atomic, and about 6.4 ns per counter write when 8 cores share the line (scaled by (threads − 1) ÷ 7 for fewer threads). With 1 thread it treats the code as the original loop: no lock, no shared counter. Real chips vary, and a real timeline is less tidy: the red and orange time is mixed into the blue, not after it. At 8 threads the work (1.0 ms) is just above the memory-bandwidth floor (about 0.93 ms), so more cores would not help much.
        
    
        Lesson 009 mode is also a simulation, using Lesson 009's numbers: Gameplay 1.4 ms (main thread only), AI 2.4 + 0.4 ms, Physics 1.0 + 1.0 ms, Animation 2.0 + 0.4 ms, Audio 0.5 ms, Particles 8.0 + 0.8 ms, Render prep 1.2 + 1.0 ms (the submit is main thread only); the first number can be split into batches (16, 8, 16 and 8), the second can't. Each job costs about 2 µs extra and each early Complete() about 0.06 ms. A simple scheduler hands the oldest ready job to the first free core (7 workers; the main thread runs its own work first and helps when there is more work than workers). Real job systems also steal work, use priorities and run things across frames, so a real timeline is less tidy.
